questions.subject: physics
questions.q: Why can two electric field lines never cross each other?
questions.answer: At the point of intersection there would be two tangents, meaning two different directions of the electric field at one point, but the field at any point has a single, definite direction.
keyPoints: Tangent to a field line gives the field direction
Crossing would give two directions at one point
The field at a point is unique
questions.explanation: A unique field direction at each point forbids intersection of field lines.

the speed with which the electric signal travels along the wire
the speed of the electromagnetic wave in the wire

They start from isolated magnetic monopoles

options: tall and wide with large area

questions.subject: physics
questions.q: Define magnetic declination and angle of dip at a place.
questions.answer: Declination is the angle between the geographic meridian and the magnetic meridian at the place. Dip is the angle that the Earth's total magnetic field makes with the horizontal at the place.
keyPoints: Declination: angle between geographic and magnetic meridians
Dip: angle of total field with the horizontal
questions.explanation: Together with the horizontal component they describe the Earth's magnetic field at a place.

questions.explanation: Wavelength is speed divided by frequency.

questions.subject: physics
questions.q: Explain how Maxwell's displacement current removes the inconsistency in Ampère's circuital law for a capacitor that is being charged.
questions.answer: Between the plates there is no conduction current, so Ampère's law applied to a surface passing between the plates would give zero while a surface cutting the wire gives a non-zero value. A changing electric field between the plates gives a displacement current equal to the conduction current in the wire, making the results agree.
keyPoints: No conduction current flows between the plates
Two surfaces bounded by the same loop gave different answers
Displacement current ε0 dΦ_E/dt equals the conduction current
questions.explanation: Adding the displacement current term makes the total current continuous.

a rarer to a denser medium at an angle of incidence greater than the critical angle
a denser to a rarer medium at an angle of incidence less than the critical angle
any medium to another at normal incidence

questions.explanation: At Brewster's angle i_B + r = 90°, so the rays are perpendicular.

most of the atom's mass and positive charge is concentrated in a tiny nucleus

the same atomic number but different mass numbers

questions.subject: physics
questions.q: Explain why the resistivity of a semiconductor decreases with temperature while that of a metal increases.
questions.answer: In a semiconductor heating breaks more covalent bonds, creating many more electron-hole pairs, so carrier density rises greatly and outweighs the extra collisions. In a metal the carrier density is almost fixed and heating increases lattice vibrations and collisions, reducing the relaxation time.
keyPoints: Semiconductor: carrier density rises strongly with temperature
Metal: more collisions, shorter relaxation time, higher resistivity
questions.explanation: Which effect dominates, carrier number or collision rate, decides the sign of the temperature coefficient.

questions.explanation: Electric field is force per unit charge, so its unit is N/C (equivalently V/m).

questions.subject: physics
questions.q: State two properties that distinguish a ferromagnetic substance from a paramagnetic one.
questions.answer: A ferromagnetic substance is strongly attracted and its atoms form domains that stay aligned; it keeps its magnetisation after the field is removed (hysteresis) and loses ferromagnetism above its Curie temperature. A paramagnetic substance is only weakly attracted and retains no magnetisation.
keyPoints: Ferromagnets: very strong attraction due to domains

questions.subject: physics

questions.answer: Eddy currents are circulating currents induced in a bulk piece of conductor by a changing magnetic flux. They are useful in induction furnaces and electromagnetic braking, and undesirable because they heat transformer cores and waste energy.

Loss: heating of cores, reduced by laminating
questions.explanation: By Lenz's law they oppose the change in flux that produces them.

is in antiphase with the voltage

questions.q: Write two uses of X-rays and one hazard associated with them.
questions.answer: X-rays are used to image bones and detect fractures and to inspect luggage and materials. They are ionising radiation, so overexposure can damage living cells.
questions.explanation: Their short wavelength lets them pass through soft tissue but be absorbed by dense material.

questions.subject: physics

questions.answer: The large refractive index gives a small critical angle of about 24°. Light entering the diamond meets internal faces at angles larger than this and undergoes repeated total internal reflection before leaving through selected faces, so much of the light is returned to the viewer.
keyPoints: Cut faces make light undergo multiple total internal reflections
Light emerges concentrated through few faces
questions.explanation: High refractive index and careful cutting maximise total internal reflection.

questions.subject: physics
questions.q: State three differences between the interference pattern of a double slit and the diffraction pattern of a single slit.
questions.answer: In interference all bright fringes have nearly equal width and intensity, whereas in single-slit diffraction the central maximum is twice as wide as the others and the intensity falls off rapidly for higher orders. Interference results from superposition of waves from two sources; diffraction from different parts of one wavefront.

Interference intensity is nearly uniform; diffraction intensity falls with order
Interference: two coherent sources; diffraction: one wavefront
questions.explanation: Both come from superposition but of different sets of wavelets.

questions.q: What did the Davisson-Germer experiment demonstrate, and how?
questions.answer: It showed that electrons behave as waves. A beam of electrons accelerated through about 54 V and scattered from a nickel crystal gave a diffraction peak at 50°, and the wavelength calculated from the crystal spacing matched the de Broglie wavelength of about 0.165 nm.
keyPoints: Electron beam scattered from a nickel crystal
Intensity peak at a definite angle like X-ray diffraction
questions.explanation: It confirmed de Broglie's hypothesis of matter waves.

questions.subject: physics
questions.q: What is nuclear fission? Give an example reaction.
questions.answer: Nuclear fission is the splitting of a heavy nucleus into two lighter nuclei, with the release of neutrons and a large amount of energy. For example, U-235 absorbs a neutron and splits into barium and krypton nuclei with three neutrons released.

Extra neutrons and large energy are released

questions.answer: An intrinsic semiconductor is pure, with equal numbers of electrons and holes produced thermally. An extrinsic semiconductor is doped with trivalent or pentavalent impurities, so one type of carrier greatly outnumbers the other and its conductivity is higher.
questions.explanation: Doping is the means of controlling the electrical behaviour of semiconductors.

questions.answer: Junction rule: the algebraic sum of currents meeting at a junction is zero, which expresses conservation of charge. Loop rule: the algebraic sum of potential differences around any closed loop is zero, which expresses conservation of energy.

questions.explanation: Aluminium is paramagnetic; bismuth, copper and water are diamagnetic.

questions.answer: The net magnetic flux through any closed surface is zero. This implies that isolated magnetic monopoles do not exist, because magnetic field lines always form closed loops.

Field lines are continuous closed loops
No isolated north or south poles
questions.explanation: Every line entering a closed surface also leaves it.

questions.subject: physics
questions.q: State Lenz's law and explain why it is consistent with conservation of energy.
questions.answer: The direction of an induced current is such that it opposes the change in flux that produced it. If it aided the change, the flux would keep growing, producing more current and energy without any work being done, which violates energy conservation.
keyPoints: Induced current opposes the change in flux
Work must be done against the opposing effect
That work appears as electrical energy
questions.explanation: The mechanical work done in moving a magnet is converted into electrical energy.

questions.subject: physics
questions.q: Why is electric power transmitted over long distances at high voltage?
questions.answer: For a given power P = VI, a higher voltage means a smaller current. The power lost in the transmission lines is I²R, so a small current greatly reduces the loss. Transformers make it easy to step the voltage up for transmission and down for use.
keyPoints: P = VI: higher V means lower I
AC allows easy voltage change with transformers
questions.explanation: Halving the current cuts the line loss to one quarter.

questions.answer: Current = 2 A; V_R = 120 V; V_C = 160 V.
questions.explanation: The voltages across R and C are 90° out of phase, so they add in quadrature.

questions.subject: physics

Ultraviolet, X-rays, visible light, gamma rays

questions.subject: physics
questions.q: Name one use each of radio waves, microwaves and infrared waves.
questions.answer: Radio waves are used for broadcasting and communication, microwaves for radar and cooking in ovens, and infrared waves for remote controls, thermal imaging and physiotherapy.
keyPoints: Infrared: remote controls or thermal imaging
questions.explanation: Each band is used according to how it is produced, absorbed and detected.

the refractive index of glass differs for different wavelengths

questions.explanation: Frequency is fixed by the source; speed and wavelength both decrease in glass.

questions.answer: A wavefront is a surface on which all points oscillate in the same phase. According to Huygens' principle each point of a wavefront acts as a source of secondary spherical wavelets, and the new wavefront at a later time is the surface tangent to these wavelets.
keyPoints: Wavefront: locus of points in the same phase
Each point is a source of secondary wavelets
New wavefront is the common tangent to the wavelets
questions.explanation: The principle explains reflection, refraction and diffraction.

Decay constant λ: decay probability per unit time
questions.explanation: A large decay constant means a short half-life.

questions.explanation: The band gap of the material determines the colour of light.

questions.q: Explain briefly the greenhouse effect in terms of electromagnetic radiation.

questions.q: State the principle of superposition and the conditions for constructive and destructive interference in terms of path difference.
questions.answer: When two or more waves meet at a point, the resultant displacement is the vector sum of the individual displacements. Interference is constructive when the path difference is nλ (n = 0, 1, 2, ...) and destructive when it is (n + ½)λ.
keyPoints: Resultant displacement is the sum of displacements
questions.explanation: These correspond to phase differences of 2nπ and (2n + 1)π.

questions.q: What is meant by the binding energy of a nucleus? Why is it released as energy when nucleons combine?
questions.answer: The binding energy is the minimum energy needed to separate a nucleus into its individual protons and neutrons. The mass of a nucleus is less than the sum of the masses of its nucleons; this mass defect Δm is released as energy Δm c² when the nucleons bind together.
keyPoints: Energy needed to separate the nucleus into nucleons
Mass defect Δm = sum of nucleon masses - nuclear mass
questions.explanation: A higher binding energy per nucleon means a more stable nucleus.

questions.q: Explain the terms depletion region and barrier potential in a p-n junction.
questions.answer: When a p-n junction forms, electrons diffuse from the n-side and holes from the p-side and recombine near the junction, leaving a region with no mobile carriers but with fixed ionised atoms: the depletion region. The fixed charges set up an electric field and a potential difference across the region, the barrier potential, which opposes further diffusion.
keyPoints: Depletion region: layer without mobile charge carriers
It contains immobile positive and negative ions
Barrier potential opposes further diffusion of carriers
questions.explanation: The barrier is about 0.7 V for silicon and 0.3 V for germanium.
